source: Original KaiSip study notes, organized by The IIA's CIA Part 1 syllabus effective 2025. KaiSip is an independent study aid, not affiliated with or endorsed by The IIA.
overview: Section B is about the person doing the audit. It covers the five behaviors every internal auditor must show: integrity, objectivity, competency, due professional care and confidentiality. These rules sit in Domain II of the Global Internal Audit Standards and bind every internal auditor, from a new hire to the chief audit executive. For each rule, learn who must act, who is told, and whether the Standards say "must" or "should".
analogy: Think of a football referee. The referee calls what they see, even against the home team with the crowd shouting (integrity). A referee whose cousin plays for one side tells the league and is swapped out (objectivity). They train every season and know the current rulebook (competency). They watch the risky parts of the pitch closely without claiming to see every foul (due professional care). What they hear in the dressing room stays there unless the rules require a report (confidentiality). A referee who fails any one of these loses the trust that makes the calls count.

topics.overview: Integrity is the base the other four ethics principles stand on. This topic covers telling the truth and speaking up under pressure, living up to the organization's ethical expectations, and staying inside the law and the profession's standards of behavior. It also shows where a concern goes once an internal auditor has seen it.
can_do: Choose the honest, complete response when a manager presses for a softer finding
Route an ethics concern or a legal violation to the party that policy and law name
Spot behavior the Standards treat as discreditable, such as an overstated credential
Explain why Domain II still binds an internal auditor who follows another ethics code

subtopics.name: Honesty and Professional Courage
subtopics.definition: Honesty and professional courage mean an internal auditor tells the truth, reports the full picture and acts on the facts, even when that is unwelcome or risky.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The board and management decide on what internal auditors tell them. A softened or missing finding leaves a risk unmanaged and destroys the trust that gives the work its value.
how_it_works: Standard 1.1 Honesty and Professional Courage requires communication that is respectful, truthful, accurate, clear and open, including when the auditor doubts or disagrees.
False, misleading or deceptive statements are forbidden. So is hiding or leaving out a finding or other relevant information.
Every material fact the auditor knows must be disclosed if silence could weaken the organization's decisions.
An auditor whose honesty or courage is tested should talk it through with a supervisor (a consideration, so "should").
The chief audit executive must keep a workplace where auditors feel supported in reporting evidence-based results, good or bad.
subtopics.example: Thabo Nkosi, an internal auditor at a water utility in Durban, finds that meter readings were estimated for months without approval. The billing manager asks Thabo to call it a small timing matter because a tariff review is under way. Thabo stays polite, keeps the finding as the evidence shows it, and tells the engagement supervisor about the request.

review: Compare draft and final communications for findings dropped without a documented reason
Trace supervisor review notes to how each challenged finding was resolved
evidence: Version history of engagement communications with the reason for each change
Stakeholder feedback on internal auditors' honesty and courage
Training records showing the ethics sessions each auditor attended
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive require a documented reason whenever a finding is removed or reworded after discussion with management.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive approves the final engagement communication

subtopics.isaca_rule: The internal auditor reports what the evidence shows, in full and with respect. Pressure, friendship or fear of consequences never justifies softening, delaying or dropping a finding.

exam_traps.trap: Dropping a minor-looking finding protects a good working relationship with the manager.
exam_traps.why: Leaving out a finding or other relevant information is forbidden. A respectful tone and fair wording protect the relationship; silence does not.

exam_traps.trap: Professional courage means confronting the manager and refusing to back down.
exam_traps.why: Courage is truthful communication and fitting action. The same standard demands respect, so the auditor listens and still reports the facts.

key_terms.definition: Doing the right thing and telling the truth by habit, even under pressure; the base for the other four ethics principles.
Speaking truthfully and acting properly when the situation is hard or the consequences are unwelcome.
A fact important enough that leaving it out could change a decision the organization makes.

subtopics.name: Meeting the Organization's Ethical Expectations
subtopics.definition: The organization's ethical expectations are the conduct standards it sets, usually in a code of conduct and related policies, which internal auditors must know, meet and help uphold.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Internal auditors can only notice and report conduct that breaks the organization's expectations if they know those expectations and the route a concern is meant to take.
how_it_works: Standard 1.2 Organization's Ethical Expectations: auditors must know the organization's legitimate, ethical expectations, live up to them and add to them.
Auditors must be able to recognize conduct that goes against those expectations, and must encourage a culture built on ethics.
An auditor who sees such conduct must report the concern as the applicable policies and procedures say, not by a private route.
If a member of senior management is involved, the chief audit executive should report it to the board; if the chair is involved, to the whole board.
Auditors should follow up on ethics matters involving the board or senior management and confirm that action was taken.
subtopics.example: During a travel expense review at a hotel group in Lisbon, internal auditor Marta Figueiredo notices a regional director approving a relative's catering invoices, which the code of conduct forbids. It is outside the engagement scope. Marta does not confront the director. Marta documents the facts and reports them to the engagement supervisor, the route the function's methodology sets.

review: Compare reported ethics concerns with the route the ethics policy sets
Sample work programs for coverage of ethics-related risks and controls
evidence: Log of ethics concerns raised by internal auditors, with dates and recipients
Each auditor's signed acknowledgment of the organization's ethics policies
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set a methodology for raising ethics concerns and align it with the board and senior management.
audit_focus.decides: Management or the board decides the response to a reported concern

subtopics.isaca_rule: The internal auditor who sees unethical conduct reports it through the channel policy sets, whatever the engagement scope. The more senior the person involved, the higher the report should go.

exam_traps.trap: The conduct is outside this engagement's scope, so the auditor can leave it alone.
exam_traps.why: The duty to report conduct that breaks the organization's ethical expectations is not tied to the scope. Staying silent fails Standard 1.2.

exam_traps.trap: A concern about a senior executive is settled by reporting it to senior management.
exam_traps.why: When senior management is involved, the chief audit executive should take the matter to the board (a consideration, so "should").

key_terms.definition: A document stating the behavior an organization expects from its people; a common home for its ethical expectations.
A workplace where doing the right thing is expected and supported at every level.
The route that policy, law or the function's methodology sets for raising a concern.

subtopics.name: Legal and Professional Behavior
subtopics.definition: Legal and professional behavior means an internal auditor obeys the law, avoids conduct that would discredit the organization or the profession, and reports violations to those who can act.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An auditor who breaks a rule, or looks away when others do, cannot credibly assess anyone else. One discreditable act can undo the standing of the whole function.
how_it_works: Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior bars auditors from anything illegal, discreditable to the organization or the profession, or likely to hurt the organization or its people.
Auditors must know and follow the laws and regulations that apply to the organization, and make any disclosures those laws require.
A violation the auditor identifies must be reported to people or bodies with authority to act, as laws, regulations and policies specify.
Discreditable acts include bullying, lying about a credential, overlooking illegal activity the organization tolerates, and an unsupported claim of conformance.
Domain II replaced the profession's earlier separate ethics code. It binds every internal auditor, even one who also follows another code.
subtopics.example: Kwame Boateng, an internal auditor at a freight company in Accra, learns that drivers' rest-hour logs are altered to hide breaches of transport law. Policy sends suspected legal violations to the general counsel. Kwame neither ignores it nor acts alone: Kwame reports the facts to the chief audit executive, who takes them to the general counsel.

review: Compare each auditor's listed credentials with the certifying body's current records
Trace reported legal violations to the authority named in policy or law
evidence: Certification status confirmations obtained from the certifying body
Documented methodology for handling legal or regulatory violations
Auditors' signed commitments to legal and professional expectations
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive document how internal auditors report legal violations when the organization's policies are not specific enough.
audit_focus.decides: Management, the board or a regulator with authority decides the response

subtopics.isaca_rule: The internal auditor stays inside the law and reports a violation to whoever has authority to act, by the route law and policy set. Tolerated wrongdoing is still reported.

exam_traps.trap: Management knows about the practice and accepts it, so there is nothing to report.
exam_traps.why: Overlooking illegal activity the organization tolerates is itself discreditable. The auditor still reports to a party with authority to act.

exam_traps.trap: Going straight to the press or a regulator is the safest first step.
exam_traps.why: Reports go to those with authority to act as laws, regulations and policies specify. An outside disclosure is made when the law requires one.

key_terms.definition: Conduct that damages trust in the auditor, the organization or the profession, whether or not a rule names it.
The Ethics and Professionalism part of the Global Internal Audit Standards, binding on every internal auditor.
The power to investigate, correct or sanction a violation.

topics.overview: Objectivity is each internal auditor's unbiased state of mind. This topic covers what objectivity is, how self-review bias, familiarity bias and conflicts of interest damage it, and how to judge whether a situation is an actual, potential or perceived impairment.
can_do: Tell an objectivity problem (the person) from an independence problem (the function) in a scenario
Judge how self-review or familiarity bias would weaken the results of a planned engagement
Decide whether a relationship, interest or past role is a conflict of interest, in fact or in appearance
Assess a former responsibility against the 12-month presumption and its advisory exception

subtopics.name: Objectivity as a Personal Mindset
subtopics.definition: Objectivity is the unbiased state of mind that lets an internal auditor judge on the evidence alone, without giving way to personal interest or to other people's wishes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Findings and conclusions are worth relying on only if bias did not shape them. Objectivity belongs to the person, so every auditor has to guard it on every engagement.
how_it_works: Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity requires an impartial, unbiased mindset in every part of the work, with judgments resting on a balanced view of the relevant circumstances.
Auditors must know their own possible biases and manage them. Bias is a normal human tendency, not proof of bad character.
Objectivity means not handing your judgment over to anyone, including senior management or others in authority.
Independence is different: it is the function's freedom from conditions that would bias its work, and it comes from reporting directly to the board.
An independently positioned function supports objectivity but cannot supply it. Each auditor still has to be unbiased.

rows.label: What it is
cells: Freedom from conditions that would bias the function's work

rows.label: Comes from
cells: Awareness of bias, disclosure and safeguards
Direct reporting to the board and proper positioning

rows.label: A problem goes to
cells: The chief audit executive or a designated supervisor
The board and senior management, from the chief audit executive

subtopics.example: At an insurer in Kuala Lumpur, Farah Aziz audits claims handling. The internal audit function reports properly to the audit committee. Farah notices they are discounting weak evidence because the claims team was so helpful last year. The function is independent, yet Farah's own view is tilting. Farah raises it with the engagement supervisor and retests the sample against the criteria.

review: Sample workpapers for conclusions that the documented evidence does not support
Compare objectivity attestations with the assignments made during the year
evidence: Supervisory review notes questioning one-sided judgments
Objectivity attestation forms signed by each internal auditor
Records of objectivity training, with participants listed
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive provide objectivity training and collect a signed disclosure attestation from every internal auditor.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides how a disclosed bias is handled

subtopics.isaca_rule: Independence is the function's; objectivity is the person's. A sound reporting line never proves that an individual auditor is unbiased, and an individual's bias is not fixed by changing the reporting line.

exam_traps.trap: The function reports to the board, so its auditors are objective.
exam_traps.why: Board reporting gives the function independence. Objectivity is each auditor's own mindset and can be impaired on any engagement, however good the structure.

exam_traps.trap: An honest auditor has no biases to manage.
exam_traps.why: The Standards treat bias as a human tendency every auditor must be aware of and manage. Denying it removes the first safeguard.

key_terms.definition: A lean in judgment, often unnoticed, that pulls a conclusion away from what the evidence supports.
Letting another person's wishes or rank replace your own professional conclusion.
Favoring no side; weighing all relevant facts in the same way.

subtopics.memory_aid: Function is independent; person is objective.

subtopics.name: Self-Review Bias and Familiarity Bias
subtopics.definition: Self-review bias and familiarity bias are two threats to objectivity: one comes from judging your own earlier work, the other from leaning on past experience instead of fresh evidence.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Both make an auditor less critical without noticing. Errors get missed, professional skepticism fades, and the engagement's results become less reliable.
how_it_works: Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity names these biases as examples, not a full list.
Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity: auditors must refrain from assessing specific activities they were previously responsible for.
For assurance, objectivity is presumed impaired if the auditor was responsible for the activity within the previous 12 months.
Familiarity grows with long or repeated work in one area and with friendly informal contact; rotating auditors between areas helps.
Staff who rotate into internal audit from the business carry self-review risk for their old areas, so safeguards should be in place.
Effect on an engagement: thinner testing, explanations accepted without corroboration, and results that others may doubt.

types.meaning: Losing a critical eye when reviewing your own work, so its mistakes and weak points go unnoticed.
Letting assumptions from past experience stand in for evidence, which weakens professional skepticism.
Misreading information because of fixed ideas about a group of people, which leads to wrong judgments.

subtopics.example: Diego Fuentes joined internal audit at a Chilean retailer eight months ago after running its accounts payable team. The plan now lists an assurance engagement on accounts payable, and Diego knows the process best. Diego was responsible for it within the past 12 months, so objectivity is presumed impaired. Diego tells the chief audit executive, who assigns other auditors.

review: Compare each auditor's prior roles with the assurance engagements assigned to them
Inspect assignment history for auditors kept on one area for years
evidence: Staffing records matched to auditors' employment history
Planning notes of the impairment discussion held before each engagement
Rotation schedule for recurring engagements
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive screen every assignment against auditors' former responsibilities and rotate staff on recurring engagements.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a delegate, decides engagement staffing

subtopics.isaca_rule: No assurance over an activity the auditor was responsible for in the previous 12 months: objectivity is presumed impaired, whatever the auditor's skill or intentions. Knowing the area best is the warning sign, not the qualification.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor who used to run the process is the best person to audit it.
exam_traps.why: Deep knowledge comes with self-review bias. Within 12 months of holding responsibility, objectivity is presumed impaired for assurance work, so someone else performs it.

exam_traps.trap: Familiarity matters only when the auditor and the manager are personal friends.
exam_traps.why: Familiarity bias is about assumptions from past experience. A long run of clean audits can dull skepticism with no friendship at all.

key_terms.definition: An impairment the Standards assume without proof, such as assurance over a responsibility held in the past 12 months.
An activity the auditor managed or was accountable for before taking up the audit assignment.
Moving auditors between areas over time so closeness to one team does not build up.

subtopics.name: Conflicts of Interest
subtopics.definition: A conflict of interest is any competing personal or professional interest, tie or activity that could sway an internal auditor's judgment, or make it look swayed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A conflict can damage confidence in the auditor, the function and the profession even when nothing improper happens, because others cannot see inside the auditor's mind.
how_it_works: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity: auditors must stay clear of conflicts of interest and must not let their own interests, or anyone else's, steer their work.
Influence can come from senior management, others in authority, the political climate or the auditor's surroundings.
Typical conflicts: interests that compete with the organization's, a chance of improper personal gain, self-protection from loss, and favoritism or nepotism.
A close personal relationship away from work, or a financial tie such as an investment, can be a conflict or look like one.
Pay can create one too, such as a bonus resting mainly on ratings from the management under review or on the number of findings.
subtopics.example: Aroha Parata, an internal auditor at a New Zealand district council, is assigned to audit a road maintenance contract. Aroha's sibling is the contractor's operations manager. Aroha owns no shares and expects to be fair. The relationship could still appear to influence the work, so Aroha discloses it to the chief audit executive before planning starts.

review: Compare auditors' declared interests and relationships with their assigned engagements
Evaluate whether auditor bonuses depend on ratings from audited managers
evidence: Conflict of interest declarations, with dates and the action taken
Remuneration plan showing how auditor performance is measured
Stakeholder survey results on how objective auditors appear
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive require conflict declarations before each engagement and remove pay measures tied to the management under review.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive determines the action on a declared conflict

subtopics.isaca_rule: A conflict of interest is judged by how it would look to a reasonable outsider, not by the auditor's own confidence. Relationships count as much as money, and appearance counts as much as fact.

exam_traps.trap: No money is involved, so there is no conflict of interest.
exam_traps.why: Family ties, friendships, favoritism and self-protection are conflicts too. The test is whether judgment could be, or appear to be, influenced.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor knows they will be fair, so nothing needs to be said.
exam_traps.why: Others may perceive an impairment even when none exists in fact. The auditor does not judge their own case; they disclose it.

key_terms.definition: Pressure or interest that pushes a judgment away from the evidence.
Favoring relatives or close friends in decisions such as hiring, contracts or ratings.
A situation that looks wrong to others, even if no improper act took place.
How an auditor is paid and rewarded; a poor design can reward biased results.

subtopics.name: Assessing Whether Objectivity Is Impaired
subtopics.definition: An impairment to objectivity is any situation, activity or relationship that may bend an internal auditor's judgments enough to change findings or conclusions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The assessment decides what happens next. Calling a real impairment harmless taints the engagement; treating every past link as a bar wastes the function's best knowledge.
how_it_works: Three kinds count: actual, potential and perceived. All must be recognized and avoided or mitigated, and none needs intent.
Assurance over a responsibility held in the previous 12 months: objectivity is presumed impaired, so the auditor stays off it.
Advisory work on a former responsibility: allowed, once the possible impairment is disclosed to the requesting party.
Assurance after advisory work: allowed if the chief audit executive confirms no impairment and staffs to manage objectivity.
Beyond 12 months the Standards give no automatic answer; the auditor judges how the assignment would look to others.

rows.label: Assurance over an activity you ran 8 months ago
cells: Objectivity is presumed impaired inside 12 months

rows.label: Advisory work on an activity you used to run
cells: Disclose the possible impairment to the requesting party before accepting

rows.label: Assurance where the function earlier advised
cells: The chief audit executive confirms no impairment and staffs to manage objectivity

rows.label: Assurance over a function the chief audit executive manages
cells: An independent party outside the function oversees the engagement

subtopics.example: Mei Tanaka, a senior internal auditor at a hospital group in Osaka, advised last year on the design of a medicine-dispensing process. An assurance engagement on it is now planned. Mei never managed the process, so the 12-month presumption does not apply. Mei still raises the advisory role, and the chief audit executive weighs it and assigns the design testing to another auditor.

review: Trace assurance engagements in previously advised areas to the documented objectivity confirmation
Compare advisory acceptances with disclosures made to the requesting party beforehand
evidence: Engagement planning files recording the impairment assessment and staffing decision
Written disclosures given to requesting parties before advisory work began
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive document the objectivity assessment before any assurance engagement in an area where the function advised.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive makes the final call on staffing

subtopics.isaca_rule: Ask three things: is it assurance or advisory, was the auditor responsible for the activity in the previous 12 months, and how would it look to others? Assurance over a recent responsibility is out; advisory work needs disclosure first.

exam_traps.trap: Disclosing a former responsibility lets the auditor go ahead with the assurance engagement.
exam_traps.why: Disclosure clears the advisory case only. For assurance within 12 months objectivity is presumed impaired, so the auditor is kept off that work.

exam_traps.trap: An auditor may never do advisory work on an area they used to manage.
exam_traps.why: Advisory work there is permitted. The condition is disclosing the possible impairment to the requesting party before the engagement is accepted.

key_terms.definition: Bias that is affecting, or has affected, the auditor's judgment.
A situation that could bias the auditor if it is not avoided or managed.
A situation others would reasonably see as bias, even if the auditor's judgment is untouched.
The stakeholder who asks for an advisory service and agrees its nature and scope.

topics.overview: Once an impairment is recognized, something has to be done about it. This topic covers the policies that protect objectivity and the options for handling an impairment: telling the right party, moving the auditor, bringing in an outside party, and refusing gifts, rewards and favors.
can_do: Decide who must be told about an impairment, and when, for an internal auditor and for the chief audit executive
Weigh reassigning, rescheduling, rescoping and outsourcing against the facts of a scenario
Judge when an engagement needs an independent party outside the function to perform or oversee it
Determine whether a gift, favor or reward must be refused under the stricter policy that applies

subtopics.name: Disclosing an Impairment
subtopics.definition: Disclosure of an impairment is the prompt reporting of its details to the party who can act on it, whether the impairment exists in fact or only in appearance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Disclosure hands the decision to someone who is not affected, so the auditor never judges their own case. Working with an undeclared impairment is itself discreditable behavior.
how_it_works: Standard 2.3 Disclosing Impairments to Objectivity: an auditor who learns of something that may impair their objectivity must tell the chief audit executive or a designated supervisor.
If it affects the work, the chief audit executive must discuss it with the activity's management, the board and/or senior management, and decide the action.
The chief audit executive's own impairment, in fact or appearance, must be disclosed to the board.
An impairment found after the engagement that makes the results less reliable, or seem so, must still be discussed and resolved.
A concern about perception alone may be discussed with management, explained and documented (a consideration).

rows.label: An auditor's own impairment
cells: The chief audit executive or a designated supervisor

rows.label: An impairment affecting the work
cells: Management of the activity, the board and/or senior management

rows.label: The chief audit executive's own impairment
Advisory work on a former responsibility
cells: The party requesting the service, before accepting

subtopics.example: Three weeks into a payroll audit at a Kenyan tea exporter, internal auditor Wanjiru Kamau starts dating the payroll supervisor. No test result has changed. Wanjiru does not wait for the engagement to end. Wanjiru discloses the relationship to the chief audit executive at once, who discusses it with senior management and decides how the engagement continues.

review: Compare disclosure dates with the dates auditors first knew of the impairment
Trace each disclosed impairment to a documented decision and its approver
evidence: Impairment disclosure register showing dates, recipients and resolutions
Board minutes recording impairments of the chief audit executive
Attestations where auditors declare an impairment or confirm none
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive define in the methodology who receives each kind of disclosure and how the decision is recorded.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides staffing; the board receives that executive's own disclosure

subtopics.isaca_rule: Disclose promptly and upward: the internal auditor to the chief audit executive or a designated supervisor, the chief audit executive to the board. The affected auditor never judges their own case.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor judges the impairment to be minor and carries on quietly.
exam_traps.why: The requirement is disclosure to the chief audit executive or a designated supervisor. Whether it affects the work is their call, not the affected auditor's.

exam_traps.trap: The chief audit executive discloses a personal impairment to the chief executive officer.
exam_traps.why: The chief audit executive's own impairment goes to the board. An administrative line to senior management does not replace the board for this disclosure.

key_terms.definition: A person the chief audit executive names to receive disclosures and oversee an auditor's work.
Reporting an impairment as soon as the auditor is aware of it, not at the end of the engagement.
Real, or reasonably seen as real by others; both trigger the duty to disclose.

subtopics.name: Reassignment and Other Staffing Options
subtopics.definition: Reassignment is taking an impaired internal auditor off an engagement and giving the work to an unimpaired one; it is one of several options for managing an impairment.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Disclosure tells the right people; it does not remove the bias. The response has to match how serious the impairment is.
how_it_works: The chief audit executive must establish methodologies for impairments. Auditors must discuss impairments and act as those methodologies say.
For an impairment that cannot be avoided, the chief audit executive may consider the options below. They are choices, not a fixed order.
When planning resources, the chief audit executive or a designated supervisor should ask the auditors about current or potential impairments, including ones disclosed before.
Those who perform and those who supervise an engagement should both be independent of the activity under review.
Reassignment fits when another competent, unimpaired auditor is available, for example after a former responsibility or a close relationship comes to light.

types.meaning: Take the impaired auditor off the engagement and assign another.
Move the engagement to a time when it can be properly staffed.
Have an outside provider perform or supervise the engagement.

subtopics.example: A bank in Jordan plans a treasury assurance engagement. Internal auditor Omar Haddad, the function's treasury specialist, discloses that a close relative was appointed head of the treasury desk last month. The chief audit executive, Rana Khoury, has two other auditors with treasury experience. Rana reassigns the engagement to them, keeps Omar off the testing, and records the disclosure and the decision.

review: Inspect planning records for the impairment discussion held before staffing
Compare the action chosen for each impairment with the documented methodology
evidence: Engagement staffing records showing reassignments and the reason for each
Internal audit plan changes showing rescheduled or rescoped engagements
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive record, for every unavoidable impairment, the option chosen and why the others were not suitable.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive chooses how an impairment is managed

subtopics.isaca_rule: The chief audit executive, not the impaired auditor, chooses the response. When a competent, unimpaired auditor is available, reassignment is usually the cleanest answer; expertise is no reason to keep an impaired auditor on assurance work.

exam_traps.trap: The impaired auditor stays on because nobody else knows the area as well.
exam_traps.why: Expertise does not cancel bias. The function can obtain the knowledge another way, through other staff, a guest auditor or an outside provider.

exam_traps.trap: Once the impairment is disclosed, the engagement can go ahead unchanged.
exam_traps.why: Disclosure starts the process. If the impairment affects the work, the chief audit executive still has to decide an action that manages it.

key_terms.definition: A step that removes a threat to objectivity or reduces it to an acceptable level.
The chief audit executive's written rules and methods for how the function works, including what to do about impairments.
One that planning cannot remove, so it has to be disclosed and managed.

subtopics.name: Outside Parties to Perform or Oversee an Engagement
subtopics.definition: Outside performance or supervision means a party from beyond the internal audit function carries out an engagement, or oversees it, because the function cannot be objective.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Some impairments reach the whole function, usually because the chief audit executive is responsible for the area. No reassignment can fix that.
how_it_works: Standard 2.3 lists outsourcing performance or supervision among the options for an unavoidable impairment.
Standard 2.2: where the chief audit executive runs a function, assurance over it needs oversight by an independent party who is not part of the internal audit function.
Standard 7.1, ongoing role: the charter records the role and safeguards, and assurance over that area comes another way, such as an outside provider reporting to the board.
Temporary role: an independent third party gives assurance over that area during the assignment and for 12 months after; the chief audit executive plans the hand-back.
Outsourcing for objectivity needs independence from the impaired person; outsourcing for skills needs expertise.
subtopics.example: At a Polish energy company the chief audit executive, Tomasz Zielinski, also runs compliance, and the charter records the role and its safeguards. An assurance engagement on compliance is planned. Senior internal auditor Ewa Nowak offers to lead it. Because Ewa reports to Tomasz, an external assurance provider performs it instead and sends its results straight to the board.

review: Compare the charter with every role the chief audit executive holds beyond internal auditing
Trace assurance over those areas to a provider outside the function
evidence: Engagement letter of the outside provider and the reports it issued
Charter section listing the added roles and their safeguards
Transition timetable for returning a temporary duty to management
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive propose to the board how each area the executive manages will be independently assured.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the added roles and acknowledges the impairment

subtopics.isaca_rule: When the impairment sits with the chief audit executive, nobody who reports to that person can cure it. Oversight must come from an independent party outside the function.

exam_traps.trap: A senior internal auditor can oversee the engagement on an area the chief audit executive manages.
exam_traps.why: Everyone in the function reports to the impaired person. Oversight must come from an independent party outside the internal audit function.

exam_traps.trap: Once a temporary role is handed back, the function can audit that area right away.
exam_traps.why: Independent third-party assurance covers the temporary assignment and the 12 months after it. A plan to return the duties to management is also required.

key_terms.definition: Hiring a provider that is not part of the organization to carry out some or all internal audit work.
Duties the chief audit executive holds apart from audit work, such as running compliance.
A provider with no reporting tie to the person or area being assessed.

subtopics.name: Gifts, Rewards and Favors
subtopics.definition: A gift, reward or favor is anything of value, tangible or not, offered to an internal auditor; it must be refused when it may impair objectivity or be presumed to.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A gift creates a sense of obligation and, even when it does not, a reason for others to doubt the results. The test is how it looks, not what the auditor intends.
how_it_works: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity: an auditor must refuse any item, tangible or not, that may impair objectivity or be presumed to impair it.
Intangible items count: hospitality, a job lead, a discount, event tickets or a personal favor.
The function's methodologies should say what is expected about gifts, favors and rewards.
The chief audit executive may set a gift policy stricter than the organization's. Auditors should follow the stricter one (a consideration, so "should").
Before accepting anything, the auditor should ask whether it could look like influence on their judgment or payment for favorable results.
subtopics.example: The organization-wide policy at a Brazilian agribusiness lets staff accept gifts worth up to 300 reais. The internal audit manual says auditors accept nothing from the management of an activity under review. After a warehouse audit, the logistics head sends internal auditor Camila Rocha a hamper worth 150 reais. Camila follows the stricter manual, returns the hamper with thanks and tells the engagement supervisor.

review: Compare gift rules for auditors with the rules for all staff
Sample gift register entries against engagements the recipients worked on
evidence: Gift and hospitality register entries for internal audit staff
Dated attestations that each auditor has read the gift rules
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive publish clear gift rules for auditors and review the register for exceptions.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive rules on any gift an auditor reports

subtopics.isaca_rule: If accepting it could impair objectivity, or lead others to presume it has, the answer is no, whatever its value. Where two policies apply, the internal auditor should follow the stricter one.

exam_traps.trap: The gift is under the organization's limit, so the auditor may keep it.
exam_traps.why: If the internal audit function's policy is stricter, the auditor should follow that one. A permitted value does not settle how the gift looks.

exam_traps.trap: Only cash or expensive items can impair objectivity.
exam_traps.why: The rule covers tangible and intangible items of any size, favors and rewards included. What matters is whether objectivity may be, or be presumed, impaired.

key_terms.definition: Something of value you cannot hold, such as a favor, an introduction, hospitality or a discount.
Reasonably assumed by others to affect judgment, whether or not it does.
The written collection of the function's methodologies that tells internal auditors how to work.

topics.overview: Competency is what an auditor knows and can do. This topic covers the rule that auditors must have, or obtain, the competencies the work needs; the professional skills the syllabus lists (communication, critical thinking, research, persuasion, relationships, handling change and curiosity); and the signs that more professional development is needed.
can_do: Apply the have-or-obtain rule when an engagement needs a skill the team lacks
Shape a message so it is accurate, clear, concise and useful to the person receiving it
Use evidence and respectful discussion to settle a disagreement with management
Recognize the signs that an internal auditor needs further professional development

subtopics.name: Competency: Have It or Obtain It
subtopics.definition: Competency is the knowledge, skills and abilities an internal auditor needs; the Standards require auditors to hold them, or get them, for the work they take on.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Work done without the right competencies gives conclusions nobody should rely on. But a skills gap is a reason to find the skill, not automatically a reason to refuse.
how_it_works: Standard 3.1 Competency: auditors must have or obtain the competencies their work needs, and take on only work they are, or can become, competent to do.
The chief audit executive must ensure the function as a whole has the competencies for the services in the charter, or obtain them.
Ways to obtain them: training, a guest auditor, hiring, other assurance providers or an external service provider (Standard 10.2).
Auditors who find an engagement's resources inappropriate or insufficient must raise it with the chief audit executive (Standard 13.5).
The Internal Auditing Competency Framework, a practice guide and not a requirement, describes four proficiency levels across four groups of competencies.

types.meaning: Aware of the subject, usually from study, with little practice in applying it.
Applies the knowledge or skill within an engagement, but is not yet ready to lead on it.
Can lead or supervise an engagement in the subject, or train others in the skill.
Shows mastery that brings real insight and foresight; a trusted advisor and a model for other auditors.

subtopics.example: The plan at a Vietnamese logistics firm includes an assurance engagement on warehouse robotics, and no internal auditor knows the subject. Engagement supervisor Linh Pham does not cancel it or staff it and hope. Linh raises the gap with the chief audit executive, who brings in an automation engineer as a guest auditor, supervised and kept off the engineer's own area.

review: Compare skills each planned engagement needs with the assigned team's documented competencies
Trace each identified skills gap to training, hiring or an outside provider
evidence: Competency assessment of the function against the internal audit plan
Contracts and qualifications of external providers and guest auditors
Training plan and budget tied to the gaps found
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive keep a current skills inventory and a documented plan to close each gap it shows.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the budget that funds training and outside expertise

subtopics.isaca_rule: Have the competency or obtain it. The internal auditor neither refuses every unfamiliar engagement nor performs one without the skills; a resource gap goes to the chief audit executive.

exam_traps.trap: The team lacks the skill, so the engagement must be declined.
exam_traps.why: The competency can be obtained through training, a guest auditor, another assurance provider or an external service provider.

exam_traps.trap: An experienced auditor can pick up an unfamiliar technical area alone during fieldwork.
exam_traps.why: Accepting work with no competency and no plan to attain it breaks Standard 3.1. Learning on an engagement is fine under proper supervision.

key_terms.definition: An expert from elsewhere in the organization who joins an engagement to supply a skill the team lacks.
An outside firm or specialist engaged to supply skills, tools or staff for internal audit work.
The combined knowledge and skills of the whole internal audit function.

subtopics.name: Communicating, Persuading and Building Trust
subtopics.definition: Communication skills are an internal auditor's ability to give the right person an accurate, clear message, in writing or speech, and to reach agreement on what the evidence means.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A correct finding changes nothing if management does not understand it, believe it or act on it. Agreement and a commitment to act show that the message worked.
how_it_works: Standard 11.2 Effective Communication names seven qualities: accurate, complete, objective, clear, concise, constructive and timely.
Fit the message to the reader: the board and senior management need different detail from the management of the activity under review.
Use the organization's own plain words and explain unavoidable technical terms.
Communicate all through the engagement, formally and informally, in writing and speech, so results are not news at the end.
Persuade with evidence. If management disagrees, auditors must discuss and seek a mutual understanding; results change only for a valid reason (Standard 13.1).
Trust grows from steady, honest contact, informal contact included, balanced against objectivity (Standard 11.1).
subtopics.example: At a closing meeting in a Canadian credit union, the lending manager rejects a finding on loan file reviews and raises their voice. Internal auditor Priya Sandhu does not argue louder or withdraw the finding. Priya walks through three sample files, listens to the manager's point about a system change, corrects one detail that was wrong, and records both positions as the methodology requires.

review: Sample final communications against the function's style guide and quality criteria
Compare the issue dates of communications with the end of fieldwork
evidence: Stakeholder survey results on the quality of internal audit communications
Supervisory review notes on drafts of engagement communications
Records of each side's position where management disagreed
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive adopt a style guide and supervisory review that test each communication against the required qualities.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides its response; the chief audit executive approves the final wording

subtopics.isaca_rule: The internal auditor persuades with evidence and respect and aims for mutual understanding, not victory. Results change only for a valid reason, never to end an argument or please a manager.

exam_traps.trap: Good persuasion means holding your position until management gives in.
exam_traps.why: The aim is a shared understanding based on evidence. An auditor who will not listen misses valid reasons to correct the results.

exam_traps.trap: Rewording a finding to satisfy an unhappy manager is good relationship building.
exam_traps.why: Relationships rest on trust and candor. Results change only for a valid reason, and a methodology lets both sides state their positions.

key_terms.definition: Worded to help the reader improve, in a cooperative tone, not to blame.
Both sides see the facts and their meaning the same way, even if they still differ on what to do.
Working through differing positions to an outcome both sides can accept, without giving up the facts.

subtopics.name: Critical Thinking, Research, Curiosity and Change
subtopics.definition: Critical thinking is reasoning from evidence to a sound judgment; with research, curiosity and readiness for change, it lets an internal auditor handle problems no checklist covers.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Organizations and risks keep shifting. An auditor who only repeats last year's steps misses new risks, accepts easy explanations and offers recommendations that no longer fit.
how_it_works: Critical thinking: use knowledge, experience and logic to judge how significant a risk is and to trace a finding to its root cause.
Problem solving: when no single fix is obvious, offer management several options, or suggest that management research the choices and decide.
Research: build understanding from several kinds of source, such as earlier engagements, risk assessments, laws, authoritative guidance, interviews, observation and data.
Curiosity: skepticism needs a willingness to look below the surface, and the chief audit executive should encourage auditors' intellectual curiosity.
Change: auditors should keep learning about trends, emerging risks and changes that affect the organization and the profession, and expect plans and methods to move.
subtopics.example: Internal auditor Nomvula Dlamini reviews customer onboarding at a South African fintech after it moved to automated identity checks. Last year's work program tests manual sign-offs that no longer exist. Nomvula reads the regulator's guidance, studies the vendor's documentation, interviews the product team and analyzes rejection data, then proposes revised test steps to the engagement supervisor for approval.

review: Sample workpapers for root cause analysis that goes beyond the visible symptom
Compare this year's work programs with last year's for changed processes
evidence: Workpapers listing the sources consulted during engagement planning
Work program revisions approved after the activity changed
Supervisor feedback on depth of analysis
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive build research time into engagement planning and coach auditors to question copied work programs.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive or engagement supervisor approves work program changes

subtopics.isaca_rule: When the situation is new, the internal auditor investigates before concluding: several sources, the root cause, more than one option. Reusing last year's work program unchanged on a changed process is the wrong answer.

exam_traps.trap: Following last year's work program exactly shows discipline and consistency.
exam_traps.why: The work program rests on current planning information. When the activity has changed, old steps test controls that may no longer exist.

exam_traps.trap: One reliable-looking source is enough to understand an unfamiliar subject.
exam_traps.why: Understanding is built from several kinds of information, and information is more reliable when another source corroborates it.

key_terms.definition: The deeper reason a problem exists; fixing it stops the problem coming back.
To confirm one piece of information with another from a different source.
The habit of asking why and wanting to learn more than the task strictly needs.
A new or changing risk whose size and shape are not yet well understood.

subtopics.name: Continuing Professional Development
subtopics.definition: Continuing professional development is the ongoing learning, through education, training and experience, by which internal auditors keep and grow their competencies after they qualify.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Knowledge goes out of date, fastest in areas such as technology and cybersecurity. An auditor who stops learning slowly loses the competency the Standards require.
how_it_works: Standard 3.2 Continuing Professional Development: auditors must maintain and keep developing their competencies and must pursue education and training.
Auditors holding professional internal audit certifications must follow those certifications' continuing education policies and meet their requirements.
Forms include self-study, on-the-job training, special or rotational assignments, mentoring, supervisor feedback, courses and conferences.
Each auditor owns their development; the chief audit executive must evaluate competencies and help through training, feedback or mentoring (Standard 10.2).
Signs of a need: a new subject or technology, a changed law or standard, critical feedback, a self-assessment gap, a new role, or stale knowledge in a fast-changing area.
subtopics.example: Senior internal auditor Hoang Minh Chau at a Singapore insurer earned a certification six years ago and has since audited only claims. A supervisor's review notes that Chau's access testing on a cloud platform relied on outdated methods. Chau does not wait for the next appraisal. Chau adds cloud security training and a mentored assignment to a development plan and agrees it with the supervisor.

review: Compare completed learning hours with each certifying body's stated minimum
Inspect performance reviews for competency gaps that led to no action
evidence: Continuing education records obtained from the certifying body or training provider
Individual development plans agreed with supervisors
Training lines in the approved internal audit budget
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set minimum learning expectations and include the cost in the budget request.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the internal audit budget, including training funds

subtopics.isaca_rule: Certification is a starting point. The internal auditor must keep developing, and a gap shown by feedback, change or a new assignment is a signal to act now, not at the next appraisal.

exam_traps.trap: Once certified, further training is a personal choice.
exam_traps.why: Continuing development is required of every internal auditor, and certified auditors must also meet their certification's continuing education rules.

exam_traps.trap: Development is the employer's job, so the auditor waits to be sent on a course.
exam_traps.why: Each auditor is responsible for their own competencies. The chief audit executive supports and funds development but does not own it for them.

key_terms.definition: Structured learning a certifying body requires holders to complete in a set period to keep a credential.
Guidance from a more experienced colleague, often while working together on real engagements.
An auditor's own schedule of the learning they will complete and by when.
An auditor's own rating of their competencies, best reviewed by a supervisor.

topics.overview: Due professional care is the standard of diligence expected of a prudent, competent internal auditor. This topic covers what care requires and does not require, the factors an auditor weighs in applying it, and professional skepticism: the questioning attitude toward whether information can be relied on.
can_do: Explain why due professional care does not mean testing everything or never missing anything
Pick out, in a planning scenario, the factors that care asks the internal auditor to weigh
Apply professional skepticism to an unsupported statement without assuming dishonesty

subtopics.name: What Due Professional Care Means
subtopics.definition: Due professional care is the level of attention, judgment and healthy doubt a sensible, capable internal auditor would apply when planning and carrying out the work.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Care sets a realistic bar. It protects those who rely on the work from sloppiness, and it protects the auditor from an impossible promise of perfection.
how_it_works: Principle 4 Exercise Due Professional Care rests on three things: conforming with the Standards, weighing the nature and circumstances of the work, and applying professional skepticism.
Auditors act in the best interests of those receiving the service, but are not expected to be infallible.
Standard 4.1 Conformance with the Global Internal Audit Standards: auditors must follow the Standards and the function's methodologies when planning, performing and communicating.
If a law blocks conformance with part of the Standards, every other part still applies and the fact is disclosed.
When a requirement cannot be met, the chief audit executive must document and communicate the circumstance, the alternative action, its impact and the reason.
subtopics.example: Sanne de Vries, an internal auditor at a Dutch pension fund, tests a risk-based sample of benefit payments, follows up every exception and has the work reviewed. A year later a fraud surfaces in a payment type the risk assessment rated low. A quality review confirms Sanne planned, tested and documented as a prudent auditor would. Care was exercised. Sanne helps update the risk assessment.

review: Sample engagements against the Standards and the function's documented methodologies
Inspect workpapers for evidence of timely supervisory review
evidence: Quality assurance and improvement program results on engagement conformance
Workpapers with dated supervisor sign-offs
Records of nonconformance disclosed, with alternative actions and reasons
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive verify, through supervision and quality reviews, that engagements follow the Standards and the methodologies.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive determines how nonconformance is documented and communicated

subtopics.isaca_rule: Due professional care is reasonable care, not a guarantee. The question is whether the internal auditor planned and worked as a prudent, competent auditor would, not whether every error was found.

exam_traps.trap: An auditor who exercises due care will find every significant problem.
exam_traps.why: Auditors are not expected to be infallible. Care is judged by the quality of the planning and the work, not by a perfect outcome.

exam_traps.trap: Care means examining every transaction to be safe.
exam_traps.why: Care weighs cost against benefit and the significance of risks. Testing everything where risk is low takes resources from higher risks.

key_terms.definition: A careful, sensible professional whose likely conduct is the yardstick for due professional care.
Never wrong; a standard the profession does not ask of internal auditors.
A requirement of the Standards that was not met; it is documented and disclosed as the Standards direct.

subtopics.name: The Factors Care Weighs
subtopics.definition: The due professional care factors are the things Standard 4.2 requires an internal auditor to assess about a service: its nature, its circumstances and what it demands.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These factors decide how much work is enough and where to point it. They tie each engagement to what the organization is trying to achieve and to its real risks.
how_it_works: Strategy and objectives: what the organization, and the activity under review, are trying to achieve.
Interests: those of the people the service is for and of other stakeholders, the public included.
Governance, risk management, and control processes: how adequate and how effective they are.
Cost against benefit: the resources the work will use compared with the value it is likely to bring.
Risk: how complex, material or significant the risks are, and how probable significant errors, fraud and noncompliance are.
The work itself: how much is needed, how quickly, and which techniques, tools and technology fit.
subtopics.example: Planning a procurement engagement at a Mexican car parts maker, internal auditor Luis Ortega walks through the vendor approval control and finds its design cannot work: one clerk both creates and approves vendors. Testing how it operated all year would take three weeks and prove little. Luis reports the design gap and proposes to the engagement supervisor that the hours move to payments, where fraud risk is higher.

review: Inspect planning notes for the organization's and the activity's objectives
Compare budgeted hours per area with the engagement risk assessment's ranking
evidence: Engagement risk assessment covering errors, fraud and noncompliance
Planning notes on the expected costs and benefits of the work
Budget-to-actual hours with reasons for variances
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive require planning notes that show how risk and cost shaped the extent of testing.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive or engagement supervisor approves the work program

subtopics.isaca_rule: Care is proportion. The internal auditor puts effort where the objectives, the risks and the likely value point, and does not spend it testing how a control operates when its design already fails.

exam_traps.trap: Cost should never limit audit work; more testing is always the careful choice.
exam_traps.why: Weighing the cost of the work against its likely benefit is one of the required factors. Effort without added value takes resources from higher risks.

exam_traps.trap: Fraud is considered only when the engagement is a fraud investigation.
exam_traps.why: How probable significant errors, fraud and noncompliance are is a factor of due professional care in every internal audit service.

key_terms.definition: Comparing what a piece of audit work will cost with the value it is likely to produce.
How large or important something is, relative to its context.
Failure to follow a law, regulation, contract, policy or other requirement.

subtopics.memory_aid: Goals, stakeholders, processes, cost, extent, significance, likelihood, tools.

subtopics.name: Professional Skepticism
subtopics.definition: Professional skepticism is a questioning attitude toward information: the internal auditor tests whether it can be relied on instead of taking it on trust.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Conclusions built on unverified statements can be wrong however carefully they are written. Skepticism keeps judgments resting on facts and logic, not on trust or belief.
how_it_works: Standard 4.3 Professional Skepticism requires it when planning and when performing internal audit services.
Stay inquisitive: curiosity and a willingness to look below the surface are part of the attitude.
Critically assess how reliable each piece of information is, including where it came from.
Raise concerns and ask about inconsistencies in a straightforward, honest way.
Seek more evidence when information or a statement could be false, misleading, incomplete or inconsistent.
Skepticism is unbiased: it assumes neither that management is dishonest nor that it is truthful. It asks for support.
subtopics.example: During an inventory audit at a Turkish textile mill, the warehouse manager tells internal auditor Elif Demir that the finance director approved all stock write-offs, though the approval emails were lost in a system migration. Elif neither accepts the statement nor accuses the manager. Elif asks the finance director directly, checks the migration logs and compares write-off patterns with earlier years.

review: Sample workpapers for management statements accepted without corroborating evidence
Trace inconsistent information noted in workpapers to its follow-up
evidence: Workpapers showing how the auditor validated information received
Supervisor review notes asking for further support
Records showing misleading information treated as a finding
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive train internal auditors to corroborate management's statements and document how each was validated.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive or engagement supervisor judges whether evidence supports the conclusion

subtopics.isaca_rule: Trust is not evidence. The internal auditor corroborates what they are told, asks openly about anything inconsistent, and stays neutral: no presumption of guilt and no presumption of truth.

exam_traps.trap: Skepticism means assuming that management is hiding something.
exam_traps.why: Skepticism is a questioning, unbiased attitude toward information. Presuming dishonesty is itself a bias and damages the working relationship.

exam_traps.trap: A senior manager's clear statement is enough support for a conclusion.
exam_traps.why: Statements are validated with evidence, not accepted because of rank. Information the auditor obtains directly or corroborates is more reliable.

key_terms.definition: A steady wish to ask questions and understand how things really work.
How far information can be trusted, given its source and whether other evidence agrees with it.
Facts or statements that do not agree with each other and so need follow-up.

topics.topic_name: Confidentiality and proper use of information
topics.overview: Internal auditors see information that few others in the organization can. This topic covers why that access brings a duty, how information may and may not be used, how it is protected through its life, and the narrow cases where confidential information is disclosed.
can_do: Apply the organization's policies, the law and the function's methodologies when handling engagement information
Recognize misuse of information, including use for personal gain that seems to harm nobody
Choose a fitting protection for sensitive information at each stage, from first access to disposal
Decide whether a request to release confidential information rests on a legal or professional duty, and who authorizes it

subtopics.name: Access to Information and the Duty of Confidentiality
subtopics.definition: Confidentiality is the internal auditor's duty to use the information they receive only for professional purposes and to keep it from anyone not authorized to have it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The mandate gives internal auditors unrestricted access to records, people and systems. People cooperate only if they trust that what auditors learn will be handled properly.
how_it_works: Principle 5 Maintain Confidentiality: auditors use and protect information appropriately.
The information is often confidential, proprietary or personally identifiable, such as salaries and personnel records.
The duty covers paper and digital records and also what is said aloud, in formal meetings or casual talk.
Ownership: the information belongs to the organization or to the people it describes, not to the auditor who reached it.
Privacy: personal data is handled as privacy law and policy require, and access is kept to what the work needs.
Unauthorized disclosure is barred inside the organization as well as outside it.
subtopics.example: Internal auditor Siddharth Rao at an Indian software company is testing payroll controls and sees the salaries of the whole leadership team. At lunch a colleague from marketing asks what the new sales head earns. The colleague is an employee but has no authorization to know. Siddharth declines, mentions nothing from the engagement, and keeps the payroll extract inside the restricted engagement folder.

review: Compare who can open engagement folders with the assigned engagement teams
Inspect signed confidentiality acknowledgments for every auditor and guest auditor
evidence: System access listings for engagement files holding personal data
Signed confidentiality or nondisclosure agreements
Attendance records for training on protecting information
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive confirm periodically that each auditor's access to information still matches what the work needs.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive confirms what access internal auditors need

subtopics.isaca_rule: Access is for the work, and for nothing else. The internal auditor shares what they learn only with people authorized to receive it, and a fellow employee is not authorized just by being an employee.

exam_traps.trap: Confidentiality is about outsiders; anything can be shared with colleagues.
exam_traps.why: Information is protected from unauthorized access and disclosure internally as well as externally. Authorization, not employment, decides who may see it.

exam_traps.trap: Only written records are confidential; a conversation is not.
exam_traps.why: The duty also covers information that comes from spoken communication, informal discussions included.

key_terms.definition: Data that can be linked to a specific person, such as a name with a salary or health record.
Information an organization owns and keeps private because it has commercial value.
The authority, given through the mandate, to reach the records, people and property the work needs.
Anyone, inside or outside the organization, without permission to receive the information.

subtopics.name: Using Information Properly
subtopics.definition: Proper use of information means an internal auditor handles it as policies, procedures, laws and regulations require, and never for personal gain or against the organization's legitimate interests.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Misuse can bring fines, reputational harm and personal liability, and it ends the trust that unrestricted access depends on. The harm does not have to be visible to be real.
how_it_works: Standard 5.1 Use of Information: whenever auditors use information, the applicable laws, regulations, policies and procedures govern how.
Using it for personal gain is forbidden, whether or not anyone appears to lose.
Nor may it be used against the organization's legitimate, ethical aims.
The rules cover the whole life of information: access, collection, transfer, storage and destruction.
Third-party information, such as a supplier's data, comes with that party's rules too.
The chief audit executive should explain the expectations and may ask for a signed acknowledgment.
subtopics.example: While auditing a planned acquisition at a listed mining company in Perth, internal auditor Jarrah Collins learns the target's name before any announcement. Jarrah's cousin trades shares and asks for tips. Jarrah could pass the name on without the company ever knowing. Jarrah refuses, buys no shares, and keeps the file in the restricted workspace as the insider information policy requires.

review: Compare auditors' personal trading declarations with engagements involving price-sensitive information
Inspect how engagement data extracts were transferred, stored and destroyed
evidence: Data transfer and deletion logs for engagement extracts
Attestation forms on information use, dated and complete for all staff
Insider list entries for internal audit staff
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive brief auditors on information-use rules and obtain each auditor's signed acknowledgment.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management sets the organization's information policies

subtopics.isaca_rule: Information gained on an engagement is used for that engagement. Personal benefit is misuse even when nobody is hurt and nobody finds out, and third-party data keeps its own rules.

exam_traps.trap: Using engagement information privately is fine as long as the organization suffers no loss.
exam_traps.why: The bar on personal gain does not depend on harm. Trading on, selling or passing on inside knowledge is the Standards' own example of misuse.

exam_traps.trap: The audit mandate overrides privacy and data protection rules.
exam_traps.why: Unrestricted access lets auditors obtain information. How they use and handle it is still governed by policies, procedures, laws and regulations.

key_terms.definition: Any benefit to the auditor or people close to them, in money or otherwise.
Financial, strategic or operational knowledge, not yet public, that could move a share price or help a competitor.
The stages information passes through, from first access to final destruction.
Data belonging to an outside party, such as a supplier or customer, that the auditor can reach.

subtopics.name: Protecting Information and Engagement Records
subtopics.definition: Protection of information is the set of steps an internal auditor takes so that information gathered in the work is not seen, copied, lost or released without authorization.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most leaks are accidents: a misdirected email, a lost laptop, an old extract nobody deleted. Auditors must manage that risk, not just mean well.
how_it_works: Standard 5.2 Protection of Information: auditors must know their protection duties and follow the laws, policies and procedures on confidentiality, privacy and information security.
The function's methodologies cover custody, retention and disposal of engagement records, and their release to internal and external parties.
They also cover confidential information, access rights and copies once these are no longer needed.
Auditors must manage the risk of exposing information by accident.
Usual protections: encryption, passwords, controlled email distribution, limits on social media use and restricted physical access.
People assisting the function, such as guest auditors and outside providers, must follow the same rules; the chief audit executive ensures it.
subtopics.example: At the end of a customer data audit at a Nigerian telecom, internal auditor Chidi Okafor still holds a file of subscriber records on a laptop and can read the billing database. The function's methodology keeps workpapers, not raw extracts. Chidi asks IT to remove the database access, deletes the extract as the methodology sets out, and notes both actions in the engagement file.

review: Compare auditors' current system access with engagements that have closed
Sample closed engagements for raw data extracts kept beyond the retention rule
evidence: Access removal records dated against engagement closure dates
Encryption status reports for internal audit laptops and shared drives
Disposal logs matched to the record-keeping schedule
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set retention, disposal and access removal steps in the methodology and monitor that auditors follow them.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive sets the function's record-handling methodology

subtopics.isaca_rule: Protect information through its whole life: limit access, secure it in use and in transit, and remove access and copies when the need ends. Good intentions do not excuse an accidental leak.

exam_traps.trap: Keeping every data extract forever is the safest way to support the findings.
exam_traps.why: Engagement documentation is retained as law and policy require. Copies and access no longer needed add exposure and are handled as the methodology says.

exam_traps.trap: Protection rules bind the function's employees, not a contractor helping on one engagement.
exam_traps.why: The chief audit executive must ensure that individuals assisting the internal audit function follow the same protection requirements.

key_terms.definition: The workpapers and other documents created or collected during an engagement.
Who holds a record and is responsible for keeping it safe.
How long a record is kept before it is disposed of, as law and policy set.
Scrambling data so only someone with the key can read it.

subtopics.name: When Confidential Information Is Disclosed
subtopics.definition: Authorized disclosure is the release of confidential information to a party entitled to it, or under a legal or professional responsibility, by the route that law, policy and methodology set.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Confidentiality is not secrecy at any price. It never justifies hiding a finding from the board, and it gives way when the law or a professional duty requires disclosure.
how_it_works: Standard 5.2: confidential information stays away from unauthorized parties unless a legal or professional responsibility calls for disclosure.
Reporting results to the board and senior management is authorized. A finding is never left out on confidentiality grounds (Standard 1.1).
Legal violations go to those with authority to act, and disclosures the law requires are made (Standard 1.3).
Before a final communication leaves the organization, the chief audit executive must first take advice, as required, from legal counsel, senior management or both (Standard 11.3).
The chief audit executive should consult legal counsel on legal requirements and protections such as privilege.

rows.label: The board asks for the full engagement results
cells: Normal reporting; nothing is held back as confidential

rows.label: A manager from another unit asks for workpapers
cells: The release rules in the function's methodology

rows.label: A law or regulation requires the disclosure
cells: As the law requires, with legal counsel's advice where needed

rows.label: A friend or a journalist asks
cells: No authorization and no legal or professional duty

subtopics.example: A bank's external auditor emails internal auditor Tala Mahe in Auckland asking for the full workpapers of a lending engagement by Friday. Tala wants to help and knows the audit partner well. Tala does not send them. Tala passes the request to the chief audit executive, who follows the function's release methodology and takes advice from legal counsel before deciding what is shared.

review: Trace each external release of engagement records to its documented authorization
Compare distribution lists of final communications with the approved recipients
evidence: Log of legally required releases and of releases cleared by legal counsel
Documented restrictions on distributing workpapers and final communications
Requests for records, with the decision and its approver
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive name in the methodology who may approve each kind of release of records.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides who receives final engagement communications

subtopics.isaca_rule: Disclose confidential information only to an authorized party or under a legal or professional duty, by the set route. Confidentiality never keeps a finding from the board.

exam_traps.trap: The matter is confidential, so the auditor leaves it out of the report to the board.
exam_traps.why: The board is an authorized recipient of results. Leaving out a finding breaks the honesty requirement; sensitivity is managed by restricting distribution.

exam_traps.trap: Confidentiality lets an auditor refuse a disclosure that the law requires.
exam_traps.why: The duty has an explicit exception for legal or professional responsibility, and auditors must make the disclosures that laws and regulations require.

key_terms.definition: A duty set by law, regulation or professional standards that requires a disclosure.
Legal protection that can keep certain communications with lawyers from being disclosed.
The function's rules for who may receive engagement records and who authorizes it.

key_terminologies.Domain II: The second domain of the Global Internal Audit Standards, on ethics and professionalism: Principles 1 to 5 and Standards 1.1 to 5.2.
key_terminologies.Integrity: Honesty plus the courage to act on the facts, whatever the pressure; the base of the other four ethics principles.
key_terminologies.Professional courage: Communicating truthfully and acting properly in a dilemma or under pressure.
key_terminologies.Discreditable behavior: Conduct that harms trust in the auditor, the organization or the profession, such as lying about a credential.
key_terminologies.Objectivity: Each internal auditor's bias-free way of thinking, which keeps judgments tied to evidence.
key_terminologies.Independence: The internal audit function's freedom to work without bias or interference, secured by reporting directly to the board.
key_terminologies.Impairment to objectivity: A situation, activity or relationship that may bias an auditor's judgment, in fact or in appearance.
key_terminologies.Self-review bias: Reduced critical thinking when an auditor reviews their own earlier work.
key_terminologies.Familiarity bias: Assumptions from past experience that take the place of fresh evidence.
key_terminologies.Conflict of interest: A competing personal or professional interest that could sway an auditor's judgment or seem to.
key_terminologies.Perceived impairment: A situation others would reasonably see as bias, even with no bias in fact.
key_terminologies.12-month presumption: Objectivity is presumed impaired for assurance over an activity the auditor was responsible for in the previous 12 months.
key_terminologies.Safeguard: A step that removes or reduces a threat to objectivity, such as reassignment or outside supervision.
key_terminologies.Designated supervisor: The person named by the chief audit executive to receive an auditor's disclosure of an impairment.
key_terminologies.Competency: What an auditor knows and can do, at the level the job needs.
key_terminologies.Continuing professional development: Ongoing education, training and experience that keep an auditor's competencies current.
key_terminologies.Due professional care: The diligence, judgment and skepticism of a prudent, competent internal auditor; reasonable care, not perfection.
key_terminologies.Professional skepticism: A neutral, questioning attitude that tests whether information can be trusted before relying on it.
key_terminologies.Confidentiality: Keeping information gained at work for work purposes alone, and away from anyone not authorized to have it.
key_terminologies.Personally identifiable information: Data that can be linked to a specific person.
key_terminologies.Methodologies: The chief audit executive's written policies and procedures for how the function does its work.
key_terminologies.Chief audit executive: The person who leads the internal audit function and answers for its quality, ethics and conformance.
key_terminologies.Engagement supervisor: The internal auditor who directs an engagement and reviews its work: the chief audit executive or someone they delegate.
key_terminologies.Board: The top governing body that authorizes and oversees internal audit; often the directors as a group, or their audit committee.
key_terminologies.Senior management: The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board for running the organization.
key_terminologies.Assurance services: Objective assessments against criteria that give stakeholders confidence about governance, risk management and control.
key_terminologies.Advisory services: Advice given at a stakeholder's request, with no assurance and no management responsibility taken on.
key_terminologies.Requirement: A part of a standard that uses "must": it is mandatory.
key_terminologies.Consideration for Implementation: A part of a standard that uses "should" or "may": preferred or optional practice, not mandatory.
